title: Working in rows and working in rounds
subtitle: The two ways crochet fabric grows
excerpt: Crochet grows in one of two ways: back and forth in rows, or outward in rounds. The choice shapes how a piece is built and how it is read. This explains the difference, how to turn at the end of a row, and how a round closes.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passages on working straight rows and on working motifs in rounds (the crochet square in rounds, Fig. 441). Public domain via Project Gutenberg.

glossaryTerms.definition: Crocheting back and forth in a straight strip, turning the work at the end of each row so the next row goes the other way.
Crocheting outward from a centre in rings, either joined at the end of each round or worked in a continuous spiral, to make a flat or tubular shape.
The chains worked at the start of a row to lift the hook to the height of the first stitch before you carry on.

content.text: Crochet grows in one of two ways.
Working in rows
goes back and forth in a straight strip, turning at each end.
Working in the round

spirals outward from a centre. Scarves, blankets, and dishcloths are usually rows; motifs, hats, and amigurumi are usually rounds. Knowing which one a pattern uses tells you how to read it and how to keep your place.
What you need
A ball of DK yarn and a 4 mm hook, enough to work a small sample of each.
A stitch marker, useful for marking the first stitch of a round or a spiral.
Working in rows
Make a foundation chain to the width you want.
Work the first row of stitches across the chain.
Turn the work so the other side faces you, like turning a page.
Work a turning chain to lift the hook to the height of the new row, then crochet back across.
Repeat the turn-and-work until the piece is as long as you want.
You will know the rows are even when the side edges stay straight and the stitch count holds the same from row to row. The
turning chain
is what keeps the edge from pulling in.
Working in the round
Start from a magic ring or a small ring of chains.
Work the first round of stitches into the centre.
Close the round with a slip stitch into the first stitch if the pattern is joined, or mark the first stitch and keep going if it is a spiral.
Work each new round outward, adding stitches as the pattern sets so the piece lies flat.
You will know a flat round is working when the piece stays flat and does not cup or ruffle. Cupping means too few stitches added; ruffling means too many.
Common mistakes
Forgetting the turning chain in rows, which makes the side edge pull in and the corners curl.
Losing the start of a spiral round. Always move the marker up into the first stitch of each new round.
Working a joined round as a spiral by mistake, or the other way round, which throws the stitch count off.
When to use it

Choose rows for anything long and flat: scarves, blankets, washcloths, rectangular wraps. Choose rounds for anything that radiates from a centre or wraps into a tube: coasters, motifs, hats, bags, and stuffed shapes. Many finished projects use both, working the body in rounds and adding a flat edging in rows at the end.
